judge/rl: GRPO, group relative policy optimization, learns from rewards: the model tries answers, and the ones that score well become more likely. Learning by trial and reward is called reinforcement learning, or RL: what pays off is reinforced.
judge/prompt: Give the model a prompt, the text it is asked to answer: nine times seven. Every answer it samples needs a reward. Who gives it?
judge/judge: One way is a learned judge: a second network, trained to score answers the way people would.
judge/hack: But that judge is a network too, and it can be wrong. Trained against it long enough, the model finds answers it scores high that are still wrong, like a confident fifty four. That is called reward hacking.
judge/checker: Here the right answer is known, so a short program can check instead. It reads the final answer and compares it with sixty three: one if they match, zero if not. Fifty four gets zero, however sure it sounds.
judge/name: A reward a program can check like this is called verifiable. In 2024, Nathan Lambert and colleagues, training their Tulu three models, named the method reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards: RLVR.
check/ans: Sample four answers to nine times seven. They end in sixty three, sixty three, fifty four and sixty three.
check/check: The checker gives one, one, zero, one. No person had to read a word.
check/code: Code is checked the same way: run each program on tests, and reward it only if every test passes.
check/r1: In January 2025, DeepSeek's R one paper trained a model called R one zero this way, with GRPO and no learned judge at all: such a judge, it found, may suffer from reward hacking.
check/format: Math answers had to put the final answer in a set place, such as a box, so a rule could find it. A second reward asked for the steps between think tags.
group/mean: These four rewards make a GRPO group. Their mean, three of four, is zero point seven five: the share that pass, called the pass rate.
group/back: It runs backwards too: eight answers with a mean reward of zero point six two five means zero point six two five times eight, five, passed.
group/std: The standard deviation, a typical distance from the mean, is about zero point four three three.
group/right: Each right answer's advantage is one minus zero point seven five, over zero point four three three: about zero point five eight.
group/wrong: The wrong one gets minus zero point seven five over zero point four three three: about minus one point seven three, a big push down.
group/scale: The size of the reward does not matter: Tulu three paid ten for a right answer, and GRPO would give these same advantages, since it divides by the spread.
edge/all: Had all four been right, every reward would equal the mean, and every advantage would be zero. All wrong, the same: that prompt teaches nothing.
edge/edge: So the prompts worth training on sit at the edge of what the model can do: it solves them some of the time.
edge/long: Only the final answer is checked, never the steps. Yet as R one zero trained, its answers grew longer, to thousands of tokens, and it began going back over its own steps.
edge/why: Nothing rewarded that directly. But whatever made a right final answer more likely was pushed up along with it.
